title: 恵美の家のきまり  (Strict Rules at Megumi's Home)

segments.t: Megumi brings Akiko home to the Sahara house, where Megumi's mother Kayo greets them in the entryway with immaculate manners. Kayo warmly offers delicious cake, yet before Akiko can take another step inside, Kayo insists she go straight to the washroom to wash her feet. Listen to the classic Japanese doorway greetings first, and notice the quiet tension underneath Kayo's gentle voice.
ただいま。
おかえりなさい。
恵美さん、ちゃんとお祈りはしてきた？
はい。
いつも教会につきあってくれてありがとう。
いえ、そんな。
おいしいケーキがありますから、上がっていってください。
お邪魔します。
足、洗わないとね。
恵美さん、お風呂場に行っていただいて。
いつもこうなの？
何が？
何でもない。
Stepping into a Japanese home comes with its own set of set-piece greetings—plus Kayo's unusually strict twist. Let's walk through each key moment.
ただいま。
'I am home.' Walking through your own front door in Japan calls for "tadaima", literally 'just now', announcing you have just returned.
おかえりなさい。
'Welcome home.' Whoever is already inside answers "okaerinasai", built on "kaeru", to return home. Family members often shorten it to warm "okaeri".
恵美さん、ちゃんとお祈りはしてきた？

'Megumi, did you say your prayers properly?' Calling your own daughter "Megumi-san" sounds strikingly formal inside a family. "Chanto" means properly or without skipping steps, and "oinori" adds respectful "o" to "inori", prayer.
いつも教会につきあってくれてありがとう。

'Thank you for always going to church with her.' "Itsumo" means always, and "kyoukai" is church. Linking "tsukiatte kurete", accompanying her for us, straight into "arigatou" thanks Akiko for a specific kindness.
いえ、そんな。

'No, not at all.' In Japan, compliments are usually deflected rather than accepted head-on: "ie" clips polite "iie", no, and trailing off on "sonna", 'nothing like that', waves the praise modestly away.
おいしいケーキがありますから、上がっていってください。

'We have delicious cake, so please come on in.' "Oishii keeki ga arimasu" says delicious cake exists here. Because Japanese entryways sit a step below the main floor, "agaru", to step up, is the everyday way to say 'come inside a home'.
お邪魔します。
'Pardon the intrusion.' Every guest crossing a Japanese threshold says "ojama shimasu"—built on "jama", getting in the way, to show respect for the host's space.
足、洗わないとね。

'You must wash your feet first, right?' "Ashi" covers both foot and leg in Japanese. Turning "arau", wash, into "arawanai to" literally says 'if you do not wash', which Japanese leaves unfinished to mean 'you have to wash'.
恵美さん、お風呂場に行っていただいて。

'Megumi, please show her to the washroom.' "Ofuroba" combines "ofuro", bath, with "ba", place. Ending softly on "itte itadaite"—humble "itadaku" for having a guest go—sounds ultra-refined yet leaves zero room to refuse.
いつもこうなの？
'Is it always like this?' Alone in the washroom, Akiko pairs "itsumo", always, with "kou", like this, and curious "na no" to ask quietly whether every day at home feels this strict.
何でもない。

'It is nothing.' Replace "nan demo", anything, with negative "nai" at the end and "nan demo nai" becomes the classic brush-off 'never mind, it is nothing'. Now let's listen to the whole entryway and washroom scene again from start to finish.
ただいま。
おかえりなさい。
恵美さん、ちゃんとお祈りはしてきた？
はい。
いつも教会につきあってくれてありがとう。
いえ、そんな。
おいしいケーキがありますから、上がっていってください。
お邪魔します。
足、洗わないとね。
恵美さん、お風呂場に行っていただいて。
いつもこうなの？
何が？
何でもない。
Those three doorway phrases—"tadaima", "okaerinasai", and "ojama shimasu", plus "agaru" for stepping up into the house—carry you into almost any home visit in Japan. See you next time.
じゃあね。
